source_text: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἵνα μὴ μόνον εἰς ἐπιτίμησιν τὸν λόγον ἀναλώσωμεν, φέρε, τὴν πρόσρησιν αὐτὴν τὴν δοκοῦσαν εἶναι περιττὴν καὶ παρενοχλεῖν, εἰς μέσον ἀγάγωμεν. Ἀναπτυσσομένης γὰρ αὐτῆς καὶ δεικνυμένου τοῦ κέρδους ὅσον παρέχει τοῖς προσέχουσιν αὐτῇ μετὰ ἀκριβείας, τότε μείζων ἔσται κατηγορία τοῖς ἀμελοῦσι τοσούτων θη σαυρῶν, καὶ τὸν πνευματικὸν ἀπὸ τῶν χειρῶν ῥίπτουσι πλοῦτον. Τίς οὖν ἐστιν ἡ πρόσρησις; Ἀσπάζεσθε, φησὶ, Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Κυρίῳ. Ἆρα οὐ δοκεῖ ψιλή τις εἶναι πρόσρησις, καὶ μηδὲν μέγα, μηδὲ γενναῖον ἡμῖν ἐνδείκνυσθαι; Φέρε οὖν, εἰς αὐτὴν μόνην ἅπασαν τὴν διάλεξιν ἀναλώσωμεν, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδὲ ἀρκέσομεν σήμερον τὰ ἐγκείμενα ἅπαντα τοῖς ὀλίγοις τούτοις ῥήμασιν ἀνιμήσασθαι σπουδάσαντες ὑμῖν νοήματα, ἀλλὰ ἀνάγκη καὶ εἰς ἑτέραν ὑμῖν ἡμέραν ταμιευθῆναι τὴν τῶν θεωρημάτων περιουσίαν, τῶν τικτομένων ἀπὸ τῆς ὀλίγης ταύτης προσρήσεως. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἅπασαν αὐτὴν ἐπελθεῖν παρασκευάζομαι, ἀλλὰ μέρος αὐτῆς καὶ ἀρχὴν καὶ προοίμιον μόνον· Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν. βʹ. Πρῶτόν ἐστιν ἐκπλαγῆναι τοῦ Παύλου τὴν ἀρετὴν, ὅτι τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν ἐγκεχειρισμένος, καὶ γῆν καὶ θάλατταν, καὶ τὰς ὑφ' ἡλίῳ πόλεις ἁπάσας, καὶ βαρβάρους, καὶ Ἕλληνας, καὶ δήμους τοσούτους ἐν ἑαυτῷ περιφέρων, ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς καὶ μιᾶς γυναικὸς τοσαύτην ἐποιεῖτο φροντίδα· καὶ δεύτερον τοῦτο θαυμάσαι, πῶς ἄγρυπνόν τε καὶ μεμεριμνημένην εἶχε ψυχὴν, οὐχὶ κοινῇ πάντων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἰδίᾳ μεμνημένος ἑκάστου τῶν δοκίμων καὶ γενναίων. Νῦν μὲν γὰρ οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν τοὺς τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν προεστῶτας τοῦτο ποιεῖν, τῷ καὶ τοὺς θορύβους κατεστάλθαι ἐκείνους, καὶ μιᾶς πόλεως ἀναδεδέχθαι πρόνοιαν μόνον· τότε δὲ οὐ τὸ τῶν κινδύνων μέγεθος μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ διάστημα, καὶ τὸ τῶν φροντίδων πλῆθος καὶ τὰ ἐπάλληλα κύματα, καὶ τὸ μὴ συνεχῶς ἅπασιν ἐπιχωριάζειν ἀεὶ, καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα πλείονα τούτων, ἱκανὰ τῆς μνήμης ἐκβαλεῖν καὶ τοὺς σφόδρα ἐπιτηδείους. Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐξέβαλε τούτους. Πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἐξεβλήθησαν; Διὰ τὴν τοῦ Παύλου μεγαλοψυχίαν, καὶ τὴν θερμὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ γνησίαν ἀγάπην. Οὕτω γὰρ αὐτοὺς εἶχεν ἐν διανοίᾳ, ὡς καὶ ἐν ἐπιστολαῖς αὐτῶν μεμνῆσθαι πολλάκις. Ἀλλ' ἴδωμεν τίνες καὶ ὁποῖοι ἦσαν οὗτοι, οἱ τὸν Παῦλον οὕτω χειρωσάμενοι, καὶ πρὸς τὸν οἰκεῖον ἐπισπασάμενοι πόθον. Ἆρα ὕπατοί τινες καὶ στρατηγοὶ ἦσαν, καὶ ὕπαρχοι, ἢ ἄλλην τινὰ περιφάνειαν κεκτημένοι, ἢ πλοῦτον πολὺν περιβεβλημένοι, καὶ τῶν τὴν πόλιν ἀγόντων; Οὐδὲν τούτων ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον ἅπαν, πτωχοὶ καὶ πένητες, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν χειρῶν ἐργασίας ζῶντες. Ἦσαν γὰρ, φησὶ, σκηνοποιοὶ τῇ τέχνῃ· καὶ οὐκ ᾐσχύνετο ὁ Παῦλος, οὐδὲ ὄνειδος εἶναι ἐνόμιζε βασιλικωτάτῃ πόλει καὶ δήμῳ μέγα φρονοῦντι, κελεύων τοὺς χειροτέχνας ἐκείνους ἀσπάζεσθαι, οὐδὲ καθυβρίζειν αὐτοὺς ἡγεῖτο τῇ πρὸς ἐκείνους φιλίᾳ· οὕτως ἦν ἅπαντας πεπαιδευκὼς τότε φιλοσοφεῖν. Καίτοι γε ἡμεῖς πολλάκις συγγενεῖς ἔχοντες πενεστέρους ὀλίγῳ, τῆς πρὸς αὐτοὺς οἰκειότητος ἀλλοτριούμεθα, καὶ ὄνειδος εἶναι νομίζομεν, εἰ φωραθείημέν ποτε ἐκείνοις προσήκοντες· ὁ δὲ Παῦλος οὐχ οὕτως, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγκαλλωπίζεται τῷ πράγματι, καὶ οὐ τοῖς τότε μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα πᾶσι δῆλον ἐποίησεν, ὅτι εἰς τοὺς πρώτους αὐτῷ τὴν φιλίαν ἐτέλουν ἐκεῖνοι οἱ σκηνοποιοί.
thought_title: The greeting to Priscilla and Aquila is not superfluous
orientation: Chrysostom is preaching on Romans 16:3, where Paul sends greetings to Priscilla and Aquila, and he is about to show that even this brief greeting contains great treasure.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed, so that we may not spend the discourse only on rebuke, come, let us bring forward the greeting itself, the one that seems to be superfluous and to cause annoyance. For when it is unfolded and the gain is shown, how much it provides to those who attend to it with precision, then the accusation will be greater against those who neglect such treasures and throw away the spiritual wealth from their hands. What then is the greeting? Greet, he says, Priscilla and Aquila, my coworkers in the Lord. Does it not seem to be some bare greeting, and to display nothing great nor noble to us? Come then, let us spend the whole discourse on this alone; rather, we will not even be sufficient today, having been eager to draw up for you all the thoughts contained in these few words, but it is necessary that the abundance of the contemplations born from this short greeting be stored up for you for another day. For I am not preparing to go through all of it, but only a part of it and a beginning and a preface: Greet Priscilla and Aquila. First it is to be amazed at the virtue of Paul, that having been entrusted with the whole inhabited world, and land and sea, and all the cities under the sun, and barbarians, and Greeks, and carrying about in himself so many peoples, he was making so much care of one man and one woman; and second, this is to be wondered at, how he had a sleepless and careful soul, remembering not only all in common, but also each one individually of the approved and noble ones. For now it is nothing wonderful for those who preside over the churches to do this, since those disturbances have been quelled and they have taken up the care of one city only; but then not only the greatness of the dangers, but also the distance of the journey, and the multitude of cares, and the successive waves, and the not always dwelling continuously among all, and many other things more numerous than these, were sufficient to cast out of memory even those who are very capable. But it did not cast out these. How then were they not cast out? Because of the greatness of soul of Paul, and his warm and genuine love. For he held them in his mind in such a way as to remember them often even in his letters. But let us see who and of what sort these were, the ones who had so captured Paul and drawn him to their own affection. Were they some consuls and generals and prefects, or had they acquired some other distinction, or had they thrown around themselves much wealth, and were they among those who led the city? None of these things can be said, but the opposite in every way: poor and needy, and living from the work of their hands. For they were, he says, tentmakers by trade; and Paul was not ashamed, nor did he consider it a reproach, in a most royal city and a people thinking great things, to command that those handworkers be greeted, nor did he consider it an insult to them by his friendship with them; so had he trained all then to practice discipline. And yet we, often having relatives who are a little poorer, estrange ourselves from closeness with them, and consider it a reproach if we are ever detected as being related to them; but Paul was not so, but he even prides himself on the matter, and made it clear not only to those then, but also to all those after, that those tentmakers were among the first in friendship to him.

choices.why: The glossary mandates 'greeting' for πρόσρησις, and it is the central term of the section.
The glossary mandates 'coworkers' for συνεργοί, and the phrase is a direct quotation from Romans 16:3.
The glossary mandates 'tentmakers' for σκηνοποιοί, and τῇ τέχνῃ specifies their occupation.
The glossary mandates 'discipline' for φιλοσοφία, and the verbal form here refers to the Christian way of life.
This renders the compound literally and captures the magnanimity Chrysostom attributes to Paul.
The two terms are near-synonyms; rendering both preserves the rhetorical doubling and the glossary's 'poverty' sense.

pass_b_english: But so that we do not spend the whole discourse only on rebuke, come, let us bring forward the greeting itself—the one that seems superfluous and intrusive. For when it is unfolded and the gain it offers to those who attend to it with care is shown, then the accusation against those who neglect such treasures and throw spiritual wealth out of their hands will be all the greater. What then is the greeting? “Greet Priscilla and Aquila,” he says, “my coworkers in the Lord” (Romans 16:3). Does it not seem to be a bare greeting, showing us nothing great or noble? Come then, let us spend the entire discussion on this one greeting alone. Or rather, we will not even be able today to draw up for you all the thoughts contained in these few words, even if we try hard; the abundance of contemplations born from this short greeting will have to be stored up for another day. For I am not preparing to go through all of it, but only a part, a beginning and preface: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila.”

First, one must be astonished at Paul’s virtue: he had been entrusted with the whole inhabited world, land and sea, all the cities under the sun, barbarians and Greeks, and he carried so many peoples within himself—yet he showed such care for one man and one woman. And second, one must marvel at this: how wakeful and attentive his soul was, remembering not only all people in common but also each of the approved and noble ones individually. For now it is no wonder that those who preside over the churches do this, since those disturbances have been calmed and they have taken on the care of only one city. But then, not only the greatness of the dangers, but also the length of the journey, the multitude of cares, the waves crashing one after another, the fact that he could not always be present with everyone continually, and many other things besides—these were enough to drive out of memory even very close friends. But they did not drive these two out. How then were they not driven out? Because of Paul’s greatness of soul and his warm and genuine love. For he held them in his mind so firmly that he remembered them often even in his letters.

But let us see who these people were and what kind of people they were, who so captured Paul and drew him to their own affection. Were they consuls and generals and prefects? Did they possess some other distinction, or were they clothed in great wealth, among those who led the city? None of these things can be said. Quite the opposite: they were poor and needy, living from the work of their hands. For they were, he says, tentmakers by trade (Acts 18:3). And Paul was not ashamed, nor did he consider it a reproach to a most imperial city and a proud people to command them to greet those craftsmen. Nor did he think he was insulting them by his friendship with those people—so thoroughly had he taught everyone then to practice discipline. Yet we, who often have relatives who are somewhat poorer, estrange ourselves from closeness with them and consider it a reproach if we are ever discovered to be related to them. But Paul was not like that. Instead, he prides himself on the matter, and he made it clear not only to those of his own time but to all who came after that those tentmakers held the first place in his friendship.

last_rejected.quote: he says, "my coworkers in the Lord" (Romans 16:3)
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀσπάζεσθε, φησὶ, Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν τοὺς συνεργούς μου ἐν Κυρίῳ
last_rejected.why: English adds "(Romans 16:3)" making Paul the epistle author; source has Chrysostom quoting Paul speaking in Romans, not citing Romans as text.
last_rejected.fix: "Greet Priscilla and Aquila," he says, "my coworkers in the Lord."
last_rejected.ruling: Source quotes Paul's words; adding reference is standard scholarly practice, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: he prides himself on the matter
last_rejected.why: "Prides himself" suggests vanity; source means he gloried in/boasted of it as honorable, not self-conceit.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐγκαλλωπίζεται includes 'prides himself/glories in'; normal range, not misleading.

problems.quote: these were enough to drive out of memory even those who were very capable
problems.source_quote: ἱκανὰ τῆς μνήμης ἐκβαλεῖν καὶ τοὺς σφόδρα ἐπιτηδείους
problems.why: Used substantivally of persons, ἐπιτήδειοι means close friends or intimates, not capable people; hardships and distance would erase even very close friends from memory.
problems.fix: these were enough to drive out of memory even very close friends
problems.ruling: ἐπιτήδειοι of persons means close intimates, not capable; context is what would erase friends from μνήμη.

edits.old: these were enough to drive out of memory even those who were very capable
edits.new: these were enough to drive out of memory even very close friends

fixed: Fixed 'those who were very capable' to 'very close friends': source τοὺς σφόδρα ἰπιτηδείους substantivally means intimates/close friends, not capable people.

problems.quote: nor did he consider it a reproach, in a most imperial city and among a people who thought highly of themselves, to command that those craftsmen be greeted.
problems.source_quote: οὐδὲ ὄνειδος εἶναι ἐνόμιζε βασιλικωτάτῃ πόλει καὶ δήμῳ μέγα φρονοῦντι, κελεύων τοὺς χειροτέχνας ἐκείνους ἀσπάζεσθαι
problems.why: The dative is not locative ('in'/'among'): Paul was not in Rome, but writing to the imperial city and proud people, commanding them to greet those craftsmen.
problems.fix: nor did he consider it a reproach to a most imperial city and a proud people when he commanded them to greet those craftsmen.
problems.ruling: πόλει καὶ δήμῳ name Rome as addressees of κελεύων ἀσπάζεσθαι; 'in/among' locates Paul there, not recipients.
